unit.title: Use graphical techniques and perform simple statistical computations (Basic)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how you would collect and count the faults found in the workshop over one month, and turn them into a frequency table.
essays.modelAnswer: First I decide what I want to find out, for example which types of electrical fault happen most often in the workshop. I make a simple record sheet with columns for the date, the machine or circuit, the type of fault and who found it, and I agree the fault types to use, such as lamp, switch, socket, breaker trip and wiring. During the month, every fault is written on the sheet as soon as it is found, in the same way each time. At the end of the month I make a tally chart: I go down the record sheet and put a tally mark against each fault type, drawing every fifth mark across the four before it, so they are easy to count in fives. Then I count the tally marks and write the totals in a frequency table, with one row for each fault type and a column for the frequency. I add up the frequencies and check that the total matches the number of faults on the record sheet.
markingPoints: Decides the purpose and agrees the fault types to count
Makes a clear record sheet (date, machine, fault type, who found it)
Records each fault at once and in the same way all month
Tallies the faults by type, counting in fives
Makes a frequency table and checks the total against the record sheet

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would draw a clear bar chart of the number of each type of fault found in a month.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the frequency table of fault types and their totals. I use graph paper, a sharp pencil and a ruler. I draw the horizontal axis for the fault types and the vertical axis for the number of faults. I choose a scale for the vertical axis that goes up in equal steps, starts at zero, and fits the largest total while using most of the paper, for example 2 faults for each large square. I label each axis, with units where needed, such as 'Number of faults'. I mark the fault types along the horizontal axis with equal gaps between them. Then I draw one bar for each fault type, all the same width, up to the height of its total, and I shade or colour them neatly. If I use colours, I add a key. I give the chart a clear title, such as 'Workshop faults, October 2026'. Finally I check each bar height against the table, and check the labels and the spelling.
markingPoints: Uses the frequency table, graph paper, pencil and ruler
Chooses an equal scale from zero that fits the data and fills the paper
Labels both axes, with units where needed
Draws bars of equal width with equal gaps, to the correct heights
Adds a title (and key if needed) and checks the chart against the table

essays.stem: Explain how to draw a pie chart for these workshop faults: lamps 12, sockets 9, breakers 6, wiring 3. Work out the angle for each sector and show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: First I add the faults to find the total: 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 30 faults. A full circle is 360°, so each fault is 360 ÷ 30 = 12°. Then I work out each angle: lamps 12 × 12° = 144°; sockets 9 × 12° = 108°; breakers 6 × 12° = 72°; wiring 3 × 12° = 36°. I check that the angles add up to a full circle: 144 + 108 + 72 + 36 = 360°. To draw the chart, I use a compass to draw a circle and mark its centre. I draw one radius from the centre to the edge as a starting line. With the protractor's centre on the centre of the circle, I measure 144° from the line and draw the next radius, then measure 108° from that line, and so on for each sector. I label each sector with the fault type and its number or percentage, or use colours and a key, and I give the chart a title, such as 'Workshop faults, October'.
markingPoints: Finds the total: 30 faults
Works out the angle for each fault (12°) or uses fraction × 360°
Correct angles: lamps 144°, sockets 108°, breakers 72°, wiring 36°
Checks that the angles add up to 360°
Draws with a compass and protractor, labels the sectors and adds a title

essays.stem: These are the times, in minutes, that seven trainees took to wire a socket outlet: 12, 15, 14, 18, 15, 16, 22. Work out the mean, median, mode and range, showing your working, and say what each one tells you.
essays.modelAnswer: Mean: add all the times and divide by the number of times. 12 + 15 + 14 + 18 + 15 + 16 + 22 = 112, and 112 ÷ 7 = 16 minutes. The mean is the average time. Median: put the times in order: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 22. There are seven values, so the middle one is the 4th, which is 15 minutes. The median is the middle time: half the trainees were quicker and half were slower. Mode: the time that appears most often is 15 minutes (it appears twice). The mode is the most common time. Range: the largest time minus the smallest: 22 − 12 = 10 minutes. The range shows how spread out the times are. Here the mean (16 minutes) is a little higher than the median (15 minutes), because the one slow time of 22 minutes pulls the mean up.
markingPoints: Mean = 112 ÷ 7 = 16 minutes, with working
Median = 15 minutes, with the times put in order
Mode = 15 minutes
Range = 22 − 12 = 10 minutes
Says correctly what each one tells you

essays.stem: Compare a bar chart, a line graph and a pie chart. Say what kind of workshop data each one suits best, with an example.
essays.modelAnswer: A bar chart uses bars of equal width, with gaps between them, whose heights show the amount in each group. It is best for comparing separate groups, for example the number of faults of each type in a month, or the number of jobs done by each team. A line graph has points plotted against a scale and joined by lines. It is best for showing how one measured value changes over time, for example the temperature of a motor every 5 minutes, or the charge of a battery over a day, because the line shows the trend and lets you read values between the points. A pie chart is a circle split into sectors, each with an angle in proportion to its share. It is best for showing how one whole is shared out, for example what fraction of all the faults were lamp faults, but it is hard to read exact values or to compare many small parts. Choosing the right graph makes the data easy to understand.
markingPoints: Bar chart: bars of equal width; compares separate groups, with an example
Line graph: plotted points joined; shows change over time, with an example
Pie chart: sectors of a circle; shows how a whole is shared, with an example
A limitation or reason for the choice (for example, pie charts are hard to read exactly)
The three are compared clearly, not just described

essays.stem: Explain how you would record a running motor's temperature every 5 minutes for 40 minutes, plot it as a line graph, and read values from the graph.
essays.modelAnswer: I set up a table with two columns, time in minutes and temperature in °C, with times 0, 5, 10 and so on up to 40. Using an infrared thermometer from a safe position, without touching the running motor or reaching past its guard, I take each reading at the same spot on the casing and write it straight into the table. On graph paper I draw the horizontal axis for time, from 0 to 40 minutes, and the vertical axis for temperature, choosing an equal scale that covers the lowest and highest readings and fills most of the paper. I label both axes with their units and give the graph a title. I plot each reading as a small cross exactly at its time and temperature, then join the points with straight lines or a smooth curve. To read a value, such as the temperature at 22 minutes, I go up from 22 on the time axis to the line, then across to the temperature axis and read the value. I can also see the trend, such as the temperature levelling off.
markingPoints: Sets up a table of time and temperature
Takes readings safely (non-contact, clear of moving parts) at the same spot each time
Time on the horizontal axis, equal scales, labels with units and a title
Plots the points accurately and joins them
Reads values between points correctly and describes the trend

essays.stem: A set of readings has one value that is much higher than all the others. Explain how this affects the mean and the median, and what you should do about it.
essays.modelAnswer: A value that is far from all the others can pull the mean a long way, because the mean uses every value. For example, job times of 12, 13, 14, 13 and 48 minutes have a mean of 100 ÷ 5 = 20 minutes, which is higher than four of the five times. The median depends only on the middle value when the times are in order (12, 13, 13, 14, 48), so it stays at 13 minutes, which better shows a typical time. The range is also made much bigger. When I find such a value, I do not just delete it. First I check whether it is a mistake, such as a misread meter, a wrong decimal point or a wrong unit, and correct it if I can. If it is a real reading, I find out why it happened, for example a faulty part or a problem during the job, and report it. In my report I can give the median as well as the mean, and say which value was unusual and why.
markingPoints: The mean is pulled towards the unusual value, with an example
The median is hardly changed, so it shows a typical value better
Checks whether the value is a recording or reading mistake; does not just delete it
If it is real, finds out why and reports it
Gives the median as well as the mean and explains the unusual value in the report

essays.stem: Explain how you would check your graphs and calculations for mistakes before you hand them in.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the data first: I compare the numbers in my table with the original record sheet to make sure nothing was copied wrongly or missed, and I check that the totals add up. I redo each calculation, if possible in a different way, for example adding a column from the bottom up, or using the calculator a second time. I check that each answer makes sense: a mean must lie between the smallest and the largest values, the percentages of a whole must add up to 100 %, and the angles of a pie chart must add up to 360°. For each graph, I check that it has a title, that both axes are labelled with units, and that the scales go up in equal steps. I check a few plotted points or bar heights against the table. I check the key and the spelling. Finally I ask another member of the group to check my work, because a fresh pair of eyes often spots mistakes that I have missed.
markingPoints: Checks the data against the original record and checks the totals
Redoes the calculations, ideally in a different way
Sense checks: mean within the range, percentages total 100 %, angles total 360°
Graph checks: title, axis labels and units, equal scales, points or bars against the table
Asks another person to check the work

essays.stem: Explain how to work out a percentage, using these two examples: 9 faulty lamps out of 150 fitted; and faults that went from 40 in March to 30 in April.
essays.modelAnswer: A percentage is a number out of 100. To work out what percentage one number is of another, I divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. For the lamps: 9 ÷ 150 = 0.06, and 0.06 × 100 = 6 %. So 6 % of the lamps fitted were faulty. To find a percentage change, I first find the change, then divide it by the starting value, and multiply by 100. For the faults: the change is 40 − 30 = 10 faults, which is a fall. 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25, and 0.25 × 100 = 25 %. So the number of faults fell by 25 % from March to April. It is important to divide by the starting value (40), not the new value (30), or the answer will be wrong. I check that my answers make sense: 6 % is a small part of the lamps, and a fall of 10 out of 40 is a quarter, which is 25 %.
markingPoints: Method: part ÷ whole × 100
Percentage change method: change ÷ starting value × 100
Faults: 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = a 25 % fall
Divides by the starting value and checks the answers make sense

essays.stem: Explain how a scatter graph can show whether two things are related. Use the example of the age of the workshop's motors and the number of faults each motor had last year.
essays.modelAnswer: A scatter graph plots pairs of values as points. For each motor, I take its age in years and the number of faults it had last year. I put age on the horizontal axis and number of faults on the vertical axis, each with an equal scale and a label, and I plot one point for each motor. I do not join the points. Then I look at the pattern. If the points tend to rise from left to right, older motors tend to have more faults: this is a positive link. If they tend to fall, older motors tend to have fewer faults: a negative link. If the points are spread all over with no pattern, there is no clear link. I can draw a line of best fit through the middle of the points to show the trend and to estimate values. A link does not always prove that one thing causes the other, but it can help the workshop decide, for example, when old motors should be replaced.
markingPoints: Plots one point for each pair of values, with labelled equal scales; points are not joined
Points rising from left to right show a positive link
Points falling show a negative link; a spread with no pattern shows no clear link
A line of best fit shows the trend and helps estimate values
A link does not always prove a cause, but helps with decisions

practical1.title: Collect workshop times and readings, work out the statistics and draw graphs
practical1.brief: As a group, collect two sets of workshop data and present them on a poster. Set 1: each member times another member (with a stopwatch or phone) as they strip and terminate five conductors into a terminal block on a dead training board, three times each, so that the group has 12 to 15 times. Set 2: measure the resistance of ten resistors or heater elements of the same stated value (not connected to any supply) with a meter, and record each value. Then: (1) record both sets on a record sheet straight away; (2) make a tally and a frequency table for the times, in 1-minute groups; (3) work out the mean, median, mode and range of the times and of the resistance readings, showing your working; (4) draw a histogram or bar chart of the grouped times, and a bar chart of the resistance readings with a line showing the stated value; (5) write two sentences saying what the results show; (6) put it all on a poster and present it to the assessor. Each member does at least one calculation, draws or checks at least one graph, and signs the work they did. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A dead training board with terminal blocks, and short lengths of conductor
Ten resistors or heater elements of the same stated value, not connected to any supply, and a meter with an ohms range
Record sheets, graph paper, a ruler, pencils and a calculator
photos: A member being timed while terminating conductors on the dead board
A member measuring the resistance of one element, with the display visible
The completed record sheet for both sets of data
The tally and frequency table for the times
The worked calculations of the mean, median, mode and range
The finished graphs, with titles, labels and scales
The finished poster, with the group presenting it
checklist: Recorded each time and reading straight away, with units
Made a correct tally and frequency table
Worked out the mean correctly, showing the working
Worked out the median, mode and range correctly
Chose a suitable graph and drew it with a title, labelled axes with units and an equal scale
Plotted or drew the values accurately
Wrote a sensible statement about what the results show
Checked another member's calculation or graph and helped correct any mistakes
Measured resistance only on parts not connected to any supply
safety: The training board used for terminating must be dead and not connected to any supply
Measure resistance only on parts that are not connected to any supply
Wear safety glasses when stripping and cutting conductors, and keep blades away from your hands
Do not rush the timed task: working safely matters more than speed
Keep the work area tidy and offcuts off the floor

practical2.title: Analyse a month's workshop fault log with a pie chart, a bar chart and percentages
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a fault log for one month from the Centre's workshop (about 40 to 60 entries, showing the date, the machine or circuit, the type of fault and the repair time). As a group: (1) sort the faults by type using a tally, and make a frequency table; (2) work out the percentage of faults of each type; (3) work out the angle for each type and draw a pie chart with a compass and protractor; (4) draw a bar chart of the fault types, with the bars in order from most to fewest; (5) work out the mean and the range of the repair times; (6) using last month's total (given by the assessor), work out the percentage rise or fall in faults; (7) write a short report for the workshop supervisor saying which faults happen most, any trend, and two suggestions to reduce faults. Each member leads one step, and every member checks at least one other member's working. Present the charts and the report to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: The month's fault log and last month's total, from the assessor
Graph paper, plain paper, a ruler, pencils, a compass and a protractor
photos: The fault log with the tally beside it
The completed frequency table with percentages
The working for the pie chart angles, with the check of their total
The finished pie chart, labelled, with a title
The finished bar chart, bars in order, with a title and labels
The calculations for the mean, the range and the percentage change
The written report for the supervisor
checklist: Sorted the faults correctly using a tally, and made an accurate frequency table
Worked out the percentages correctly and checked their total
Worked out the pie chart angles correctly and checked their total
Drew an accurate, labelled pie chart with a title
Drew a bar chart in order, with equal bars, labelled axes and a title
Worked out the mean and range of the repair times correctly
Worked out the percentage change from last month correctly
Wrote a clear report naming the most common faults, with two sensible suggestions
Checked another member's working and helped correct mistakes
safety: Use the compass point carefully and keep it away from faces and hands
Keep the work area tidy so nobody trips over bags or chairs
Take short breaks during long spells of calculating and drawing
If the group visits the workshop to check the log, follow the Centre's rules there and wear the PPE required
